title: LN2-immersion memory pods with 77K-retuned low-Vt access transistors
idea: Borrowing from cryo-CMOS built for quantum-computer control, retune the access transistor for 77 K: subthreshold slope steepens from ~80 to ~20 mV/dec, so Vt can drop ~0.4 V and the wordline from ~3 V to ~1.5 V while off-current still falls >1000x. DIMMs run immersed in boiling liquid nitrogen (made from air, no chokepoint) with refresh stretched from 64 ms to minutes.
why: Facts 3 and 10: refresh tax (16-33% of idle power, 10-20% of bandwidth) goes to near zero and wordline CV^2 roughly quarters; cryoplant overhead must stay below the saving, which favors large AI memory pods.

title: Coulomb-blockade quantum-dot islands as the access switch
idea: Spin-qubit fabs already pattern ~5 nm silicon islands; put an array of ~100 parallel sub-3 nm Si dots in series with the storage node so the single-electron charging energy (>10 kT at room temperature at that size) blocks transport unless the wordline aligns the dot levels. Off-current then falls exponentially with charging energy instead of riding the thermionic subthreshold tail.
why: Fact 3: an off-state set by a Coulomb gap rather than Vt could cut the leakage tail >100x and remove most refresh; the parallel dot array is needed to reach ~0.5 uA on-current for 10 ns writes.

title: Downhole-grade amorphous Ga2O3 BEOL access transistor
idea: Oil-well electronics survive 200 C with wide-bandgap channels; deposit an amorphous Ga2O3 channel (4.8 eV gap vs IGZO ~3.2 eV) below 400 C as a vertical BEOL access device over the capacitor array. Generation leakage scales roughly as exp(-Eg/2kT), so off-current at 85 C should sit orders of magnitude below IGZO and silicon.
why: Facts 2 and 3: retention of minutes even when hot, so refresh nearly disappears, and the access device moves to low-temperature deposition that stacks in 3D; risk is low mobility (~1-10 cm2/Vs) and contact resistance.

title: Venus-lander vacuum nanogap field-emission access switch
idea: Vacuum electronics are the switches that survive Venus' 460 C surface; build each access device as a vertical ~10 nm sealed vacuum gap with a sharp emitter on the storage-node side and a gate ring, so electrons cross by field emission only when the wordline raises the tip field. Off, there is no channel, junction or trap to leak through.
why: Fact 3: junction and subthreshold leakage are gone (only exponentially suppressed Fowler-Nordheim tunneling remains), giving near-static, temperature-immune retention; hermetic nanogap sealing and emitter wear are the risks.

title: Rad-hard SOI trick: buried plate swung negative in standby
idea: Satellite SOI chips tune transistors through the substrate; build the array over a buried plate (SOI or deep n-well) under all access channels and drive it to about -2 V whenever a subarray idles, raising Vt ~150-200 mV, then to 0 to +0.5 V when the bank opens to boost drive current.
why: Fact 3: ~10-50x lower subthreshold leakage in idle subarrays lengthens refresh intervals by a similar factor, and active-mode forward bias lets the access device shrink; cost is the plate charging energy per bank open.

title: LLM decode sweeps counted as refresh: implicit-refresh accounting
idea: In AI inference each decode token reads the whole live KV cache every ~20-60 ms, and every activation restores its row. A per-row last-activated timestamp in the controller marks rows a sweep recently touched and drops them from the refresh schedule, so only cold rows get explicit refresh.
why: Facts 3 and 8: for KV-cache-dominated HBM most explicit refresh disappears, recovering most of the 10-20% bandwidth refresh takes at 32-64 Gb, with no device change.

title: Ephemeral-grade DRAM: sell retention rejects to frame-buffer users
idea: Camera, display and network ring buffers overwrite every byte within ~16 ms. Create a product grade for dies that fail the 64 ms retention screen but pass at 16-32 ms, sold to customers whose controllers guarantee a rewrite cadence and issue no refresh at all.
why: Scarce supply: turns retention-fail scrap and downbins (a few % of output) into usable bits, and these buyers spend zero refresh energy; adds supply without a new fab.

title: Pacemaker-style adiabatic refresh recycling charge between subarrays
idea: Implants live on nanowatts by never dumping charge to ground. During refresh, pair a subarray whose bitlines must rise with one whose bitlines must fall and move charge between them through a stepwise switched-capacitor ladder, so each refresh recovers roughly half of the bitline CV^2 instead of discarding it.
why: Fact 3: refresh energy (~46 fJ/bit) could drop ~40-60% and self-refresh standby power with it, for a few % more periphery area.

title: Reactor surveillance-capsule canary cells that age ahead of the array
idea: Reactor vessels carry test specimens placed to age faster than the vessel itself. Put canary cells in every bank with deliberately weakened isolation (shorter gate, thinner spacer, higher junction field) so they lose data and wear 3-5x faster; the controller sets refresh from when canaries fail, tracking a 30-year industrial life.
why: Fact 3: replaces a worst-case-plus-margin 64 ms schedule with a measured, aging-aware one, typically 2-4x less refresh early in life while staying safe as traps accumulate.

title: Automotive LDMOS drift region at the storage-node junction
idea: Automotive power MOSFETs handle hundreds of volts by spreading the field over a lightly doped drift region. Give the access transistor's storage-node side a short graded drift extension with the buried-wordline edge acting as a field plate, so the peak field that drives GIDL and trap-assisted tunneling falls ~30-40%.
why: Fact 3: the <=13 fA tail comes from high-field trap-assisted tunneling, which depends exponentially on field, so tail-cell leakage could drop ~10x and the tail-set refresh interval stretches accordingly.

title: Phone-sleep charge overdrive: boosted restore before self-refresh
idea: Phones spend >90% of their time in standby. When memory enters self-refresh, write back every row once with the array voltage boosted ~1.3x (and wordline boost to pass it), storing ~30% more charge so cells take longer to droop to the sense threshold, then self-refresh at a proportionally slower rate.
why: Fact 3: ~1.5-2x lower self-refresh rate in standby, the phone's biggest DRAM energy term; dielectric stress and higher leakage at high stored voltage limit it to sleep only.

title: Hibernation-latch ferroelectric gate: Vt parked high in deep idle
idea: Rosetta's spacecraft slept 31 months. Add a thin ferroelectric layer to the buried-wordline gate stack that is polarized only when a bank enters or leaves a long idle state (minutes to hours), shifting access Vt up ~0.4 V while hibernating and back when active; flips happen per hibernation, not per access, so ~1e6 cycles suffice.
why: Fact 3: idle banks of cold data (most server memory at any moment) get ~1e4 lower leakage and almost no refresh, without the endurance wall that ruled out per-access ferroelectric switching.

title: Particle-detector correlated double sampling: decay-tracking reference cells
idea: Detector front-ends subtract a reference sample taken under identical conditions. Each subarray keeps reference cells written with 1 and 0 at the same moment as the data rows and refreshed with them; the sense reference is set at the midpoint of the decayed reference pair instead of a fixed VBL/2.
why: Fact 3: as stored ones droop the reference follows, so cells stay readable down to much lower residual charge, plausibly a 2-3x longer refresh interval and better temperature tolerance.

title: Hearing-aid tunnel-FET access device with sub-60 mV/dec switching
idea: Zinc-air hearing aids run near 1.2 V, which pushes designers toward band-to-band tunneling switches. Use a vertical heterojunction TFET (Ge source, Si channel in the pillar) as the access device: its modest on-current still charges 5 fF in ~10 ns, and its steep slope lets the wordline swing shrink while off-current falls to sub-fA.
why: Facts 3 and 10: wordline swing ~3 V to ~1.5 V (~4x less wordline CV^2) and ~10x smaller leakage tail; drain-side ambipolar leakage must be suppressed with asymmetric doping.

title: Smart-dust Esaki-diode latch that makes the DRAM cell static
idea: Smart dust has no energy budget for refresh. Hang two series tunnel (Esaki) diodes between the rails at the storage node; their negative-differential-resistance curve gives two stable points near 0 and VDD, so pA-level diode currents hold the node instead of letting it decay, while reads and writes still use the normal access transistor.
why: Fact 3: refresh disappears (the cell becomes static like tunnel-diode SRAM) at a fraction of SRAM area; risk is building matched nanoscale tunnel diodes inside a 6F^2 footprint and their standby current.

title: Junctionless access nanowire: predictable decay for cold-boot-proof vaults
idea: Secure-key vaults want memory that decays on a known schedule, which needs a tight leakage distribution. Use a uniformly doped junctionless nanowire access device: with no metallurgical p-n junction there is no junction field peak or dopant-gradient trap zone, so the trap-assisted-tunneling outliers that form the leakage tail largely vanish.
why: Fact 3: refresh is set by the tail, not the median; compressing the tail toward the median could lengthen worst-case retention 5-10x, with a 'decays in N seconds' secure-memory product as a bonus.

title: Detector-grade crucible-free float-zone wafers for leak-free arrays
idea: Particle detectors use float-zone silicon grown without a quartz crucible, with ~100x less oxygen and few oxygen-vacancy traps. Develop 300 mm float-zone (or crucible-free pedestal-grown) substrates for DRAM array wafers so oxygen-precipitate generation centers near the access junction are gone.
why: Resources and fact 3: removes the Spruce Pine high-purity-quartz crucible dependency for array wafers and shrinks the retention tail; 300 mm FZ growth is unproven and oxygen-free wafers lose some mechanical strength.

title: EMP-hardened NEMS relay access switch with air-gap off-state
idea: Military and nuclear electronics use nanomechanical relays because radiation and EMP do not affect them. Build a vertical NEMS cantilever relay per cell that touches the storage-node contact only when the wordline pulls it in; off, an air gap gives zero subthreshold and junction leakage.
why: Fact 3: capacitor dielectric leakage becomes the only loss, giving near-static retention; risks are contact wear (>1e14 cycles needed in hot rows), stiction and 10-50 ns mechanical switching.

title: Space-CCD bakeout: on-die heaters anneal leakage traps in field
idea: Space telescopes periodically heat their CCDs to anneal radiation-induced traps. Embed resistive heaters in the package or under each bank and, after migrating data away, bake the array at ~150-200 C for minutes a few times a year to anneal variable-retention-time traps and re-passivate interface states.
why: Fact 3: the VRT and tail population that forces refresh guardbands grows with age; periodic anneal resets it, keeping refresh intervals long over life and cutting guardband ~2x.

title: Global-shutter pinned storage node borrowed from image sensors
idea: Image sensors hold photo-charge in pinned memory nodes for hundreds of ms with dark current of a few electrons per second, by burying the n storage region under a p+ pinning layer that keeps it away from the Si/SiO2 interface. Build the DRAM storage-node junction as such a pinned structure so interface-state generation is screened off.
why: Fact 3: surface and junction generation leakage could drop >10x, leaving channel leakage, which Vt can fix; fitting the pinning layer into 6F^2 is the challenge.

title: Record-solar-cell passivated contact at the storage-node junction
idea: Record silicon solar cells reach junction saturation currents of ~1-5 fA/cm2 with a ~1.5 nm tunnel oxide capped by doped polysilicon (TOPCon). Form the capacitor-to-access-device contact the same way, so the heavily doped, defective region sits in the poly rather than in the silicon and contact-region generation current collapses.
why: Fact 3: attacks contact-region generation and trap-assisted tunneling, a tail contributor; solar fabs show the process is cheap and high-volume, so it is a low-capital addition.

title: Hyperscaler fleet learning: refresh set from wafer-map telemetry
idea: A hyperscaler runs millions of DIMMs. Log correctable-error and retention telemetry against each die's fab ID (lot, wafer, X-Y) to build a fleet model of retention by wafer position and process lot; new DIMMs get per-bank refresh rates from that model at install, with no slow per-row profiling.
why: Fact 3: ~2-4x average refresh reduction for most dies (edge-of-wafer and weak lots keep 64 ms), sold back to DRAM vendors as a yield-learning data service.

title: ReLU-sparsity polarity mapping: zeros stored in the non-leaking state
idea: AI activation tensors are 50-90% zeros after ReLU. Map the dominant value to the cell state that cannot leak (discharged node, using true/complement bitline placement plus a per-row invert bit) and keep a per-row all-discharged flag so the controller skips refresh for rows holding no charged cells.
why: Fact 3: only charged cells need refresh, so for sparse AI data refresh energy drops by roughly the sparsity fraction (2-5x).

title: Deep-space LDPC pages: refresh at the 1% retention quantile
idea: CCSDS deep-space links decode reliably near 1e-2 raw BER. Store each 4 KB page as one LDPC codeword (~15% parity, decoder in the HBM base die or CXL controller) and set refresh where 1% of cells have decayed instead of where the last 1e-9 tail cell does; the median retention distribution is far longer than the tail, so the interval grows from 64 ms to ~1-2 s.
why: Fact 3: refresh energy and bandwidth loss fall ~15-30x and per-row profiling and VRT guardbands are no longer needed; costs ~15% parity and decode latency hidden behind page-granular access.

title: KV-cache significance split: mantissa tails in unrefreshed rows
idea: LLM KV caches tolerate noise in low-order mantissa bits. Keep sign, exponent and top mantissa bits in normally refreshed ECC rows, and put the low 4-5 mantissa bits of each BF16/FP8 value in rows refreshed only at their 1%-BER age with no ECC, so softmax sees those flips as tiny noise.
why: Facts 3 and 5: ~30-40% of KV bits drop most refresh and all parity, cutting HBM refresh energy and ECC overhead; expected perplexity change <0.1%.

title: SEU-style bit interleaving turns clustered weak rows into random errors
idea: Rad-hard memories interleave codeword bits across distant cells so one particle strike flips at most one bit per word. Spread each codeword over the chips and subarrays that are activated together, so a weak row, a VRT cluster, a bad access-transistor column or a hammered row adds at most one bit per codeword, keeping errors iid at the 1% cell BER the code is sized for.
why: Facts 3 and 9: a cheap code handles 1% raw BER without being beaten by correlated failures, and row-hammer flips are absorbed without per-row counters, saving periphery area.

title: Downhole adaptive code rate: parity grows as the die heats
idea: Oil-well tools swing 25-200 C and cannot afford refresh that doubles every ~10 C. Keep refresh fixed and let raw BER float from 0.01% up to 1%; an on-die thermometer steps each page's code rate from 0.97 down to 0.85, borrowing spare capacity from a reserved pool when hot.
why: Fact 3: refresh energy stays flat across temperature instead of rising 4-8x when hot; capacity rather than energy absorbs heat, which suits AI servers running memory at 85-95 C.

title: $1 IoT sensor log repaired by signal smoothness, not ECC
idea: Cheap sensor nodes log slow physical signals (temperature, vibration, ECG). Their embedded 1T1C macro has no ECC and refreshes only at its 1%-BER age (seconds); firmware delta-encodes samples and a Hampel/median filter at read removes physically impossible isolated jumps, using the signal's physics as the code.
why: Cost and fact 3: an ECC-free, rarely refreshed embedded DRAM replaces SRAM at ~5x density in low-cost MCUs, and refresh, often the sleep-power floor, nearly vanishes.

title: Spacecraft residue-number codes for error-tolerant numeric storage
idea: Fault-tolerant spacecraft arithmetic used redundant residue number systems. Store integers and quantized weights as residues modulo small coprimes plus two redundant moduli in rows running at 1% BER; a corrupted residue is located and corrected via the Chinese Remainder Theorem, and add/multiply run on residues without decoding.
why: Facts 3 and 5: refresh drops to the 1% quantile and the same redundancy protects in-memory arithmetic; ~25-35% overhead, competitive with ECC because compute stays carry-free.

title: Insect-drone hyperdimensional memory in rarely refreshed banks
idea: Tiny drones use hyperdimensional computing, where items are 10,000-bit random vectors that stay recognizable with 10-30% bit flips. Hold the associative item and class hypervectors in banks refreshed only when raw BER reaches ~1%, re-bundling vectors from recent samples now and then.
why: Fact 3: for HDC workloads refresh energy and ECC almost vanish and 1% cell BER costs no accuracy, so cheaper, leakier cells can be used.

title: Satellite data-carousel memory: detect, then refetch the golden copy
idea: Broadcast satellites loop data so receivers fill gaps. Treat DRAM as a 1%-BER cache of data that also lives in NAND or CXL far memory: each 4 KB block has a CRC plus a light code that fixes most errors, uncorrectable blocks are refetched from the golden copy, and DRAM refreshes only at its 1% age.
why: Fact 3: for read-mostly data (weights, page cache, embeddings, roughly half of server DRAM) refresh falls ~10x and parity stays ~3-5%, since rare failures cost a refetch, not a stronger code.

title: Space-AI noise training: models learn to ignore 1% weight flips
idea: Satellite AI on commercial hardware is trained with fault injection. Fine-tune LLM and vision models with random 1% bit flips injected into stored weights (with exponent clamping at load), producing weights that run from unrefreshed, ECC-free DRAM at 1% cell BER with negligible accuracy loss.
why: Fact 3 and supply: weights are 50-80% of inference memory; dropping 12.5% ECC and most refresh frees capacity and energy with no hardware change.

title: RFID-cheap transistorless crosspoint capacitors with MIIM tunnel selectors
idea: Penny RFID tags use two-terminal tunnel structures. Replace the access transistor with a back-to-back metal-insulator-insulator-metal tunnel selector (~1e6-1e8 I-V nonlinearity) in a 4F^2 crosspoint of stacked capacitors; half-selected cells leak and disturb, giving ~1% raw BER that page coding absorbs.
why: Facts 2 and 4: no transistor means no lateral-transistor blocker for 3D and no EUV access layer, with 4F^2 stacked tiers for 2-4x density per mask; refresh is frequent, so it fits streaming and ephemeral data.

title: Printed-electronics nanoimprint access layer with 1% dead cells allowed
idea: Flexible-electronics makers accept defect rates an EUV fab never would. Pattern the access-transistor and buried-wordline layers by step-and-flash nanoimprint (~$1-2M tools vs ~$200M EUV) and treat the ~0.5-1% of defective or leaky access devices from template defects as a known error budget the page code absorbs.
why: Fact 4: removes 2-3 of the 5-7 EUV layers at the densest array levels, cutting capital and depreciation (~55% of wafer cost) perhaps 20-30%.

title: QLC-flash lesson: two-bit-per-cell DRAM at 1% symbol errors
idea: NAND moved to 4 bits per cell by accepting high raw BER plus strong LDPC. Store four charge levels per DRAM capacitor with a two-step coarse/fine sense amp, refresh when level spacing decays to the 1%-error point, and decode with the page code.
why: Cost per bit: ~2x bits per cell (~1.7x net after parity and slower sensing) without more tiers or EUV layers; refresh rises ~2-3x, offset by the 1%-quantile policy.

title: CubeSat COTS mindset: half-charge capacitors in short 30:1 pillars
idea: CubeSats fly cheap commercial parts and absorb upsets in software. Size the cell capacitor for a 1% raw-BER sense margin (~2-2.5 fF) instead of ~5 fF, so pillar aspect ratio drops from ~65:1 to ~30:1 with standard high-k.
why: Fact 1: steps back from the capacitor charge wall; fewer deep-etch and deposition steps raise yield and cut cost, and short capacitors ease 3D tiers, with refresh at the 1% point roughly offsetting the lower charge.

title: AR-glasses budget: drop the negative-wordline pump and cut VPP
idea: AR glasses have milliwatt memory budgets. Lower the wordline high from ~3 V to ~2.2 V and remove the negative-wordline charge pump, lowering access Vt to keep write speed; the higher off-current and occasional incomplete writes push raw BER toward 1%, which the code tolerates.
why: Facts 7 and 10: pumps run at ~30-40% efficiency, so wordline energy falls ~45%, pump area shrinks a few % of the die, and gate-oxide and GIDL stress drop.

title: DirectFlash for DRAM: hyperscalers buy raw, retention-unscreened dies
idea: Some all-flash array vendors buy raw NAND and manage it themselves. Hyperscalers likewise buy DRAM dies that skip hot retention test, laser repair and retention binning, at a discount, and run them behind their own LDPC/CXL controller sized for 1% cell BER.
why: Cost and supply: retention test and burn-in tie up costly testers and scrap marginal dies; moving that job into the buyer's code adds several % usable supply and cuts test cost per bit.

title: Trusted-foundry domestic metals: tungsten-free TiN or poly buried wordlines
idea: Defense trusted foundries prize domestic materials. Replace tungsten in buried wordlines with TiN-only or heavily doped polysilicon; the higher RC makes far-end access devices turn on late and leaves some cells partly restored (~0.5-1% raw BER near row ends), which the code absorbs instead of finer wordline segmentation.
why: Resources: removes a China-~80% tungsten dependency from the array (contacts can move to U.S.-mined molybdenum) at no density cost, with a modest throughput hit at row ends.

title: Probe-style closed-loop power control applied to refresh pacing
idea: Space probes tune transmit power from receiver feedback to sit just above the error target. Make each row group's refresh period a control loop: the decoder reports corrected-bit counts per page, and the controller lengthens or shortens that group's period to hold raw BER near a 0.5-1% setpoint, following temperature, aging and VRT without profiling.
why: Fact 3: refresh follows each group's real decay instead of the global worst case, about 2x below a fixed 1%-quantile schedule, with built-in safety.

title: CD-player C2 flags: sense amps that mark uncertain bits as erasures
idea: CD players mark scratched symbols as erasures so the decoder can fix twice as many. Give the bitline sense amplifier a third 'uncertain' output (a window comparator about +/-20 mV around the reference) so weakly decayed cells reach the decoder as erasures rather than silent errors, doubling correctable bits per parity bit.
why: Fact 3: at fixed parity, refresh can stretch further, or the same 1% cell BER needs about half the parity; costs a few transistors per sense amp.

title: Lossy NUMA node standard: OS pages tagged by error tolerance
idea: Push a JEDEC/CXL descriptor that publishes each region's raw-BER-vs-refresh curve, plus a Linux 'lossy NUMA node' reached with mmap(MAP_LOSSY). KV caches, media buffers and caches go to 1%-BER regions refreshed rarely; kernel and databases stay on fully protected memory.
why: Supply and fact 3: makes 1%-BER memory a standard, procurable class so the other tolerance tricks deploy across vendors; government AI-cluster procurement can require support.

title: Implant-free Schottky source/drain access devices from flexible electronics
idea: Flexible electronics cannot use high-temperature implant anneals, so they rely on Schottky metal contacts. Build the DRAM access transistor with silicide Schottky source and drain (no junction implants, no activation anneal), accepting its higher thermionic off-leakage and a 1% raw BER from the weakest cells.
why: Facts 2 and 4: drops implant and anneal steps and allows low-temperature access devices in stacked 3D tiers, easing a 3D DRAM blocker; refresh at the 1% quantile keeps refresh near today's level.

title: QLC-SSD poly-channel stacking: 3D DRAM tiers on NAND's process
idea: 3D NAND reaches 300+ layers with leaky, variable poly-Si channels because controllers absorb ~1e-2 raw BER. Build vertical-bitline 3D DRAM with poly-Si lateral access devices deposited in the stack, accepting grain-boundary leakage and variability as ~1% raw BER handled by page LDPC.
why: Fact 2: existing NAND fabs (depreciated tool sets, some in the U.S.) could make 3D DRAM tiers without single-crystal Si/SiGe epitaxial stacks, making the ~26-tier break-even reachable.

title: Solar-industry kerfless epitaxial wafers: no quartz crucible needed
idea: Solar makers grow wafers directly on porous-silicon templates and lift them off, with no crucible. Use kerfless epitaxial or UMG-seeded substrates with heavy gettering for DRAM array wafers, accepting ~10x shorter carrier lifetime and higher junction generation leakage as errors inside the 1% budget.
why: Resources: removes high-purity quartz crucibles (Spruce Pine >80%) and much CZ crystal capacity from array wafers; substrate cost could fall ~2-3x.

title: HFT-overclocker truncated restore: cut tRAS, let weak cells fail
idea: High-frequency traders overclock and accept margins others refuse. Shorten the restore phase of activate and refresh (tRAS and tWR ~30-40% shorter) so slow tail access transistors leave cells partly charged; the code absorbs the resulting ~1% errors, and partly restored rows are queued to refresh first.
why: Facts 3 and 8: lower access latency and ~30% less refresh time and restore energy, recovering refresh bandwidth and row-cycle time with no device change.
